edges.description: Uncontrolled alveolar replication produces a diffuse pneumonia with impaired gas exchange.
Alveolar trophic attachment and host inflammatory injury directly manifest as diffuse alveolar pneumonia.
Diffuse alveolar exudate and impaired gas exchange produce progressive dyspnea and hypoxemia.
The host alveolar and systemic inflammatory response to Pneumocystis jirovecii infection produces fever.

nodes.description: Progressive dyspnea with hypoxemia is characteristic of PCP.

P. jirovecii depends on de novo folate synthesis. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole inhibits this pathway (sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase; trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase), and is the first-line treatment and prophylaxis. (This antifolate target is analogous to the bacterial folate pathway but is not modeled here as conforming to the bacterial folate module, since Pneumocystis is a fungus.)

nodes.description: Pneumocystis jirovecii is an opportunistic fungal pathogen that causes severe pneumonia in immunocompromised hosts. Disease requires impaired cell-mediated immunity — HIV (where CD4+ T-cell depletion <200 cells/µL is the classic marker), organ transplantation, malignancy, and inflammatory/rheumatologic conditions and their immunosuppressive therapies (which impair broader cell-mediated immunity beyond CD4 count alone) — permitting uncontrolled alveolar replication.

nodes.description: Co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole) inhibits the folate-synthesis pathway (DHFR and dihydropteroate synthase, respectively); it is the first-line treatment and prophylaxis for Pneumocystis pneumonia. Alternatives for intolerance or treatment failure include dapsone, atovaquone, pentamidine, and clindamycin-primaquine.
